I am seventy-six years old, and I have been farming this same land in Quzhou County since I was a young man. My bones ache in the morning, and my eyes are not what they used to be, but I still know every inch of my five mu of contracted land. I only went to primary school, so I do not read books about farming—I read the soil, the sky, and what my neighbors are doing. This year, like every year, I will stick to the wheat-maize rotation that has fed my family for decades.

In the autumn I already sowed winter wheat, and now that spring has come I am watching it green up. I use the improved variety Luyuan 502—my neighbors say it is reliable, and I have seen it give me about 500 kg per mu when the weather cooperates. Before sowing I rotary-tilled the soil to break up the stubble and level the field. I put down compound fertilizer as a base dressing, and when the wheat revives after winter I topdress with urea. In total I use about 17 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus some phosphorus and potassium. I will irrigate three times: once before winter to help the seedlings establish, once at jointing when the wheat starts shooting up, and once at grain filling so the grains plump up. I spray pesticides four times through the season to keep away rust, aphids, and weeds.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant summer maize. At my age I cannot afford to waste time or labor tilling again, so I direct-seed the maize into the wheat stubble with no-tillage. I plant Denghai 605—it is a hybrid seed that gives good yields, usually around 550 kg per mu. Maize needs less fertilizer than wheat; I apply about 11 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus a little phosphorus and potassium with the base fertilizer. I irrigate twice during the summer if the rains do not come, and three pesticide sprays are enough to control the borers and weeds.

I do not experiment with new crops or fancy techniques anymore. My children work in the city and send money home, but this land is my responsibility and my pride. The wheat-maize system is what the land here was made for, and as long as my legs can carry me to the field, it is what I will grow.
